reason: The neighboring surface cells and junctions suggest a first step toward a protective skin barrier.
expectation: The junctions should connect the surface cells into a more cohesive layer.

effect: The junctions made a connected sheet, but water still escapes, so the surface needs another barrier.
reaction: The edge-tug illustration clearly shows what the junctions do.
reason: The tough outer layer has overlapping cells and lipids that look suited to reducing water loss from the exposed sheet.
expectation: The outer layer should cover the connected cells and reduce water loss.

effect: The outer layer reduced water loss and showed that living cells beneath replace the dead surface cells. The skin still needs support and sensory endings.
reaction: The comparison of water arrows makes the barrier's role clear.
reason: The skin support cells and connective fibers look like parts of a supporting layer beneath the surface.
expectation: They should form a supportive skin layer that can be joined to the surface barrier.

effect: The support cells and collagen formed a layer with capillaries; it can now support the surface barrier.
reaction: The tug panels make the fibers' supporting role clear.
reason: The supporting layer and surface barrier appear to be complementary parts of the skin.
expectation: They should form a supported skin barrier that can receive sensory endings.

effect: The surface and supporting layers now form layered skin, with vessels beneath the living surface cells. It still needs sensory endings.
reaction: The vessel inset helps show how the layers relate.
reason: The sensory endings belong beneath the skin surface and should add the ability to sense contact.
expectation: The endings should create skin that can sense touch while limiting water loss.

effect: The skin now detects contact, but the dashed gap shows its sensory route still needs connection to the nervous system. The arm also needs continuing supplies.
reaction: The gap makes the remaining connection clear.
reason: The arm already has a connection to the central nervous system, so attaching the sensitive skin should connect touch information to it.
expectation: The skin should cover the arm and connect its touch signals to the nervous system.

effect: Touch signals now reach the spinal cord, but the arm's supply connection is still missing.
reaction: The separate insets make the remaining supply connection clear.
reason: The body supply network carries oxygen and nutrients, and the arm has unconnected vessel ends.
expectation: The circulation should connect to the arm and supply its muscle and skin cells.

effect: The arm now has nerve connections and continuing supplies from the circulation. The remaining goal is to use contact feedback to hold the glass.
reaction: The separate nerve and blood arrows clearly show their different roles.
reason: The living body model and glass are the available pieces for the new goal.
expectation: The model should use touch feedback to hold the glass steady.

effect: The final result shows how touch feedback and muscle activity help steady a slipping glass, completing the chapter's goals.
reaction: The slipping-and-correction sequence makes the purpose of the sensory connection concrete.

mostWorthwhile.text: Holding the glass brought the skin, nerves and muscles together in a familiar action. The sequence showed why touch feedback matters.

leastWorthwhile.text: Joining the supporting layer to the surface was straightforward, though the result's vessel gap did not itself explain how supplies cross it.

surprise.text: The outer layer slows water loss without making skin completely waterproof, and living cells replace its dead surface cells.

arbitrary.text: None of the combinations felt arbitrary; the item descriptions and goals gave each a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would be interested in another chapter if it continued connecting cell and tissue functions to familiar actions. The glass sequence made those connections more engaging than assembling layers alone.
